questions.title: Does an employee have standing to sue for civil penalties under the MFLSA when those penalties are payable to the state?
questions.question_body: In *Bruce Cohen v. Consilio*, the Seventh Circuit vacated summary judgment on the MFLSA penalties claim on jurisdictional grounds, citing concerns about standing. The opinion references *Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw* and emphasizes that penalties payable to the government must still provide a "redress to citizen plaintiffs." I'm confused: under the MFLSA, can a private employee directly sue for the statutory civil penalties, or must the claim be asserted by the state commission? How do the standing requirements of *Laidlaw* apply to the MFLSA context, and what precedent governs this issue in the Eighth Circuit?

questions.title: What is the procedural effect of a stipulation that an employee has been paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages before summary judgment?
questions.question_body: The parties in *Cohen v. Consilio* stipulated that Cohen had been paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages owed under the MFLSA, yet the court still needed to address the penalty issue. Does such a stipulation foreclose the court from considering the penalty claim, or does it merely narrow the issues for summary judgment? How does the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure treat stipulations of payment when the plaintiff seeks additional statutory remedies?

questions.title: Why does Minnesota Statute § 181.101 limit penalty enforcement to the Commissioner, and can an employee bypass the Commissioner to seek penalties directly?
questions.question_body: The opinion explains that § 181.101 authorizes only the Commissioner to serve a demand and collect penalties, and that the collected money must go to the employee. In *Cohen v. Consilio*, the court held that Cohen cannot directly sue for average daily wage penalties under the MPWA. I'm trying to understand the statutory construction: does the language of § 181.101 expressly preclude an employee from an independent civil action for penalties, or is this a matter of legislative intent inferred from the existence of a separate penalty‑seeking provision in § 181.13?

questions.title: How does the Eighth Circuit determine mootness for statutory penalty claims when the alleged wrongful conduct has been allegedly cured?
questions.question_body: In the opinion, the court discusses that if Consilio's overtime policy is no longer in effect, Cohen's MFLSA penalty claim may be moot. What legal standard does the Eighth Circuit apply to decide whether a penalty claim is moot? Specifically, how does the court balance the deterrent purpose of civil penalties against the fact that the underlying conduct may have ceased, and are there any prior Eighth Circuit cases that address this tension?

questions.title: Can a plaintiff amend the form of injunctive relief sought after filing the complaint, and what are the limits under Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a) as applied in *Cohen v. Consilio*?
questions.question_body: Cohen initially asked for specific injunctive relief, then later changed his request to a broader rescission of the overtime policy in his summary‑judgment briefing. The appellate court said the issue was not properly before it because new relief requests must be raised via an amended complaint. How does Rule 15(a) govern such changes in injunctive relief, and does the timing of the amendment (i.e., after summary judgment briefing) affect the court’s discretion to allow it?

questions.title: What is the standard for granting summary judgment on state wage‑law claims in federal court, and how did the district court apply it in *Cohen v. Consilio*?
questions.question_body: The district court granted summary judgment on the MPWA, MFLSA, and MWTA claims. I'm trying to grasp the de novo review standard used by the Eighth Circuit for summary judgment in federal courts when state wage statutes are at issue. What burden must the moving party meet, and what level of evidence is required to show that there are no genuine issues of material fact on the employee's entitlement to penalties under these statutes?
